one_liner: Rust CLI hex dumper that uses multiple threads, SIMD and mmap to dump large files far faster than xxd, hexyl and hexdump.
what_it_does: fasthex is a standalone command-line hex dumper (`fasthex [options] file`). Its default output is a hexdump -C style canonical view (8-digit offset, 16 hex bytes, |ASCII| panel), not xxd's grouped 2-byte layout. It also has flags that mirror xxd and hexdump: -p (plain hex), -i (C include array, 12 bytes per line like xxd -i), -r (reverse to binary), -o/-d/-b (octal, decimal, binary), -w (squeeze repeated rows), hexdump-style -e format strings, colour schemes and borders. It is a tool, not a library; there is no API to call from other code.
how_it_is_fast: When given a single mmap-able file, it maps the file and has rayon format output chunks in parallel (about 16 MiB of output per chunk in the current code). A separate writer thread drains finished buffers while the next chunk is formatted, using a 6-buffer pool. Hot rows are formatted with hand-written x86-64 intrinsics: AVX-512BW, then AVX2 at 32 bytes (2 rows) per call, then SSSE3/SSE4.1 at 16 bytes. Kernels are chosen at runtime with is_x86_feature_detected, and a std::simd nibble-LUT kernel is used on nightly builds. On Linux it also calls madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL/WILLNEED/HUGEPAGE) and writes through a private pipe with vmsplice+splice when stdout is a regular file or FIFO.
when_to_use: Dumping very large files (hundreds of MiB to tens of GiB) on a multi-core x86-64 Linux box, where xxd (~35 MiB/s in the README run) takes minutes
Producing canonical hex+ASCII dumps into a file or pipe for grep/diff, where the vmsplice/splice path and parallel formatting both apply
Quick -p plain-hex or -i C-array generation from big binaries when xxd is the bottleneck
Interactive `fasthex file | less` on huge files, where it keeps up with paging far better than single-threaded dumpers
when_not_to_use: Scripts that parse xxd's exact output: the default layout is hexdump -C style, not xxd's `7f45 4c46` 2-byte grouping, and -p writes the whole file as one unbroken hex line (xxd -p wraps at 60 hex chars), so it is not byte-compatible.
Input from stdin or several files concatenated: that goes through the single-threaded streaming path (4 MiB buffers, no rayon), so most of the headline speedup does not apply
Small files or `-w` squeeze / `-m` max-lines runs: squeeze and max-lines force a serial path, and on small inputs thread and mmap setup costs are all overhead

When correctness matters more than speed: the ~4,650-line main.rs has no unit tests (only a CI smoke check of -p against od on 4 KiB of random data), about 100 `unsafe` uses, and SECURITY.md itself lists 'SIMD paths producing different results than the scalar fallback' as a risk

Non-Linux or non-x86 hosts: the zero-copy output, MADV_HUGEPAGE and the hand-written intrinsics are Linux- or x86-64-only. aarch64 and macOS builds exist but get the portable or scalar kernels and plain writes. Windows is not in the release matrix.

integration.dependencies: memmap2 0.9, rayon 1.12, libc 0.2, clihelp 0.1 (binary crate; install via `cargo install fasthex`, AUR fasthex / fasthex-bin, Nix flake, or GitHub release binaries)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 (so 1.85+). crates.io releases are built and smoke-tested on stable; rust-toolchain.toml pins nightly, which enables the std::simd portable_simd kernel detected by build.rs.
integration.platforms: Release binaries for x86_64/aarch64 Linux (gnu and musl) and x86_64/aarch64 macOS. SIMD kernels need x86-64 (SSSE3/SSE4.1 minimum, AVX2/AVX-512BW used if present); vmsplice/splice and MADV_HUGEPAGE are Linux-only. Windows is not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable (CLI process). Internally it uses rayon's global pool for formatting plus one writer thread; there is no documented flag to set the thread count.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces xxd/hexdump for viewing and has xxd-like -p/-i/-r flags, but the default output format differs from xxd, and flag semantics are its own

gotchas: The README says the zero-copy path works 'regardless of what stdout is (/dev/null, ...)', but the code only enables vmsplice/splice when stdout is a regular file or FIFO. /dev/null is a character device, so the benchmark runs used plain write(), which is already almost free on /dev/null.
The input is mmap'd with memmap2 (`unsafe Mmap::map`). Truncating or rewriting the file while it is being dumped can SIGBUS the process or give inconsistent output.

The octal and minimal fast paths only engage while displayed offsets stay at or below 0xFFFFFFFF, so dumps of files over 4 GiB in those modes fall back to slower kernels. Older versions, including the one that ran the 69 GiB benchmark, wrapped offsets past 4 GiB.

Default colouring is `auto`: on a TTY it emits ANSI colours and takes the slower coloured path. Use --color=never for apples-to-apples timing. The FASTHEX_DEFAULT_OPTS environment variable is silently prepended to argv.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The hex siblings (const-hex, zbjornson fast-hex, eddieantonio's hx NEON kernel) are in-process encode/decode libraries that produce bare hex strings. Pick fasthex when you want a ready-made xxd/hexdump-style CLI dump of big files with offsets and an ASCII panel. Pick const-hex or fast-hex when you need hex encoding inside your own Rust or C++ code.
verified_claims_summary: These are the author's own hyperfine wall-clock numbers, from the README table last changed 2026-06-12. Dumping a 1.5 GiB file to /dev/null took 0.78 s for fasthex against 43.62 s for xxd, 53.14 s for hexyl --color=never and 116.03 s for hexdump. That is about 1.9 GiB/s input for fasthex vs about 35 MiB/s for xxd (derived). A 69 GiB file took ~1 min vs ~1 h 30 m for hexyl. The rig is an Intel T-series desktop: the gist says 'i5-7700T', which is not a real SKU, and earlier README revisions say i5-7500T. It had 16 GB RAM and a 990 Pro NVMe, and ran with no Rust version, build flags, tool versions or benchmark script published. After the 3 warmups the 1.5 GiB file most likely sits in page cache, so the result compares parallel SIMD formatting against single-threaded formatters, not I/O.
status_note: Actively developed by a single author: first commit 2026-04, last commit 2026-09-18, crates.io 0.3.28 with 451 downloads and 13 stars. Several releases were yanked (0.3.23–0.3.27) after stable-build breakage, and the benchmarks predate much of the current code. It is Apache-2.0 and easy to install from crates.io or AUR, but it is young and has little test coverage.
